Aelred of Rievaulx
AL-red uv ree-VOH
n. (1110–1167, English Cistercian abbot of Rievaulx, author of Spiritual Friendship)
Aelred, Old English Æthelræd, noble counsel; of Rievaulx in the North Riding.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Aelred was born at Hexham, son and grandson of married priests of the old English church, and was raised at the court of David I of Scotland, where he rose to be steward. About 1134 he turned aside to the new Cistercian house at Rievaulx in Yorkshire and stayed; he was made abbot in 1147 and governed some six hundred and fifty men until his death in 1167. His writings are unusually warm for the century: the Mirror of Charity, a life of Edward the Confessor, and above all Spiritual Friendship, which takes Cicero's treatise and rebuilds it on Christ. This dictionary records Aelred because the subject he made his own is one the Bible treats seriously and the church often does not. Scripture gives friendship a definition with a cost in it, “A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity” (Pro 17:17), and a ceiling, “Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends” (Joh 15:13). It names such a bond at its height, “the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David” (1Sa 18:1), and insists the honesty in it will sometimes hurt, “Faithful are the wounds of a friend” (Pro 27:6).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines friendship as attachment to a person proceeding from esteem; a friend as one attached by affection; affection as a bent of mind toward a particular object; charity as love and good will; and adversity as a state of affliction.

expand to see more

FRIENDSHIP, n. An attachment to a person, proceeding from intimate acquaintance, and a reciprocation of kind offices, or from a favorable opinion of the amiable and respectable qualities of his mind.

FRIEND, n. One who is attached to another by affection; one who entertains for another sentiments of esteem, respect and affection, which lead him to desire his company.

AFFECTION, n. A bent of mind towards a particular object, holding a middle place between disposition and passion.

CHARITY, n. In a general sense, love, benevolence, good will; a disposition of heart which inclines men to think favorably of their fellow men.

ADVERSITY, n. An event or series of events which oppose success or desire; misfortune; calamity; affliction; distress.

Key Scripture

Pro 17:17 — "A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity."

Joh 15:13 — "Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends."

1Sa 18:1 — "And it came to pass, when he had made an end of speaking unto Saul, that the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul."

Pro 27:6 — "Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful."

Modern Corruption

Cistercian abbot of Rievaulx, 1110–1167: wrote the century's best book on friendship and governed six hundred men with it.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that friendship is a serious Christian subject with a biblical shape. Scripture makes constancy the test rather than enjoyment, “A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity” (Pro 17:17), and lets the Lord set the measure at the only place it can finally be set, “that a man lay down his life for his friends” (Joh 15:13). Aelred was right that a cloister full of men needs this taught, and so does a congregation.

The live distortion is a sentimental friendship that cannot say anything hard. Aelred insisted that a friend who flatters is no friend, which is Solomon's own position, “Faithful are the wounds of a friend” (Pro 27:6). The great biblical instance involves a man surrendering a throne to the friend who would take it, “the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David” (1Sa 18:1). That is costly and clear-eyed, and it is not what most people mean by the word.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew rea' (H7453), a friend; Greek philos (G5384), a friend; Hebrew qashar (H7194), to knit together; Hebrew petsa' (H6482), a wound; Greek agape (G26), love.

expand to see more

Hebrew rea' (H7453) — a friend, a companion; “A friend loveth at all times”, Proverbs 17:17.

Hebrew tsarah (H6869) — distress, the brother's proper hour; “a brother is born for adversity”, Proverbs 17:17.

Greek philos (G5384) — a friend, the object of greatest love; “that a man lay down his life for his friends”, John 15:13.

Hebrew qashar (H7194) — to bind, to knit soul to soul; “the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David”, 1 Samuel 18:1.

Hebrew petsa' (H6482) — a wound, dealt in faithfulness; “Faithful are the wounds of a friend”, Proverbs 27:6.

Usage

"“A friend loveth at all times” (Pro 17:17) — constancy as the test."

"“that a man lay down his life for his friends” (Joh 15:13) — the ceiling Aelred would not lower."

"“Faithful are the wounds of a friend” (Pro 27:6) — why flattery disqualifies."
